title: Best AI Agent Builders for Sales Workflows in 2026: 8 Platforms Compared
summary: Compare eight platforms for building AI agents for lead qualification, account research, outreach and CRM updates in 2026: how you build an agent, what it can write to your CRM, how you review its work, and what it costs.
body_markdown:
Last verified: November 16, 2026


**An AI agent for sales is a model that is given a goal, a set of tools and access to your data, and decides on its own which steps to take: research an account, score it against your ICP, draft the first email, update the CRM.**


A workflow runs the steps you wrote down. An agent picks the steps. That is the whole difference, and it is also the whole risk: the agent is only as good as the data it reads, the tools it is allowed to call, and the review that catches it when it is wrong.


So the useful question is not “which platform has agents?”. Almost all of them do now. The useful questions are these four:


1. **How do you build the agent?** A no-code builder, a chat you teach, a template, or code you can review.
2. **What can it read and write?** Which CRM, natively or through a connector, and whether it can change records or only read them.
3. **How do you see and stop what it does?** Run history, approval before actions, tests, versions and rollback.
4. **How is it priced?** Seats, credits, tasks or executions change what a busy agent costs.


The eight platforms below answer those four questions differently. Every claim about another vendor comes from that vendor’s own product, docs or pricing pages, checked on November 16, 2026, and listed in the sources at the end.


## Quick answer#


**Cargo is the strongest fit for technical teams that want sales agents to run on shared GTM data, be reviewed as code, and leave a trace of every run.** Agents are declared in a TypeScript project or built in the UI, read your models and context, call the same tools your plays and reps use, and answer in plays, Slack, Chrome, LinkedIn, Notion or on a schedule.


Choose **Relevance AI** for the widest set of prebuilt sales-role agents and explicit multi-agent teams; **n8n** when self-hosting and a blank canvas matter most; **Agentforce** when Salesforce is the system of record and agents should write to it natively; **HubSpot Breeze** when your CRM is HubSpot and you want agents with no integration work; **Clay** when the agent’s job is account research and enrichment at scale; **Lindy** when a rep wants to delegate tasks in chat without designing anything; and **Zapier** when you want an AI step inside automations you already run.


## AI agent builders for sales compared#


Platform How you build an agent CRM access Review and control Price type


**1. Cargo** TypeScript project or UI; coding agents can write it for you HubSpot, Salesforce and others through maintained connectors, read and write Plan before deploy, versions and rollback, per-run traces, evaluators, alerts Platform plan + usage credits

## 1. Cargo#


Cargo is go-to-market infrastructure for coding agents. An agent on Cargo is one primitive among the others (data models, context, tools, plays, territories, apps), and that is the point: the agent reads the same account record, the same ICP definition and the same tools as everything else in the engine.


**How you build it:** Declare the agent in your Cargo project with its model, instructions, the models it may read and the tools it may call, then` cargo-ai project plan` shows the change and` deploy` applies it. Or ask Claude Code, Cursor or Codex to write it; they produce the same code in your repository. The UI builds the same agent for people who prefer it, with a test chat before release.


**What it reads and writes:** Agents read unified models (companies, contacts and deals merged from CRM, warehouse, product and billing) and the context repository, where your ICP, personas and playbooks live as versioned files. They act through tools: enrichment waterfalls, web search, and the HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack and other connectors your workspace has, including CRM writes with deduplication and protected fields.


**Where it runs:** As a step in a play on a trigger, mentioned in a Slack thread, in the Chrome side panel, answering replies on LinkedIn, on Notion comments, or on a cron schedule declared with the agent.


**How you see what it did:** Every run is a trace of each tool call with its duration and cost. Evaluators grade output and gate what passes, alerts fire on failed runs or steps, and agents keep memory across runs. Because the agent is code, a change to its instructions or tools is a pull request with a diff, and a bad release is a rollback.


**Where it breaks:** If one rep wants an agent this afternoon to draft follow-ups, Cargo is more system than you need; Lindy, HubSpot Breeze or a Relevance AI template will be live faster. Cargo gives the most leverage when someone owns the architecture and reviews changes. Its prebuilt agents ship as cookbooks (account scoring, email conversations with leads, Ask Cargo) rather than a large marketplace of sales roles.


**Pick it when:** Agents are becoming part of your revenue infrastructure, not a side tool. You want them on the same data and rules as your plays, built and changed through code review, and traceable when a lead was scored or routed wrong.


## 2. Relevance AI#


Relevance AI calls itself “the home of the AI Workforce”: a low-code platform for building AI agents and multi-agent teams.


**How you build it:** Three starts: describe the agent and let it generate one, clone a prebuilt agent from the marketplace, or build from scratch, adding actions with a no-code tool builder. A JavaScript SDK and API exist for teams that want code. Sales templates include a research and enrichment agent, a pre-meeting prepper, an outbound prospector and a deal reviewer.


**Multi-agent:** Agents link on a visual canvas into a “workforce”, each handling one part of a multi-step process. Of the platforms here, it makes the most explicit claim about coordinating several agents.


**Control:** Human-in-the-loop approvals, role-based access, real-time monitoring, agent tracing with OpenTelemetry export, version control and audit logs.


**Where it breaks:** The agent is the product, not the data layer under it. Account identity, deduplication and the commercial rules your agents should share live wherever your CRM and other tools keep them. Its public pricing is also unclear: the docs list self-serve plans metered in actions and vendor credits, while the pricing page shows only an enterprise contract.


**Pick it when:** You want prebuilt sales agents and multi-agent teams with enterprise governance, assembled mostly without code.


## 3. n8n#


n8n puts agents and workflows on one spectrum: “The less of the process you can define, the more agent you need.”


**How you build it:** A visual builder with code steps whenever you need them, an AI Assistant that drafts agents, an MCP server, and thousands of community templates. Workflows can become tools for an agent, and agents can call sub-agents.


**What it reads and writes:** Native HubSpot and Salesforce nodes create, update and upsert contacts, companies, leads, deals and opportunities, and can be handed to an agent as tools. It lists 500+ native integrations.


**Control:** Human approval per action, replay of sessions and tool calls, execution logs, evaluations and built-in versioning; Enterprise adds diffs and audit logs. n8n can run in its cloud or self-hosted, with source on GitHub.


**Where it breaks:** n8n moves data between nodes; it does not supply the commercial model behind it. Your team defines account identity, ownership, protected CRM fields, territories and why an account was prioritized. That freedom turns into infrastructure work as the number of agents grows.


**Pick it when:** Self-hosting or data control is a requirement, your team is technical, and you already own the data model. Per-execution pricing also makes high-volume, many-step agents cheaper than per-step meters.


## 4. Salesforce Agentforce#


Agentforce is Salesforce’s agent platform, with prebuilt SDR and sales coach agents and agents you build yourself.


**How you build it:** Low-code Agent Builder, Agent Script, pro-code Apex and JavaScript, Flows, Prompt Builder and MuleSoft connectors. It advertises multi-agent orchestration.


**What it reads and writes:** Native Salesforce CRM and Data 360. Sales agents update opportunity fields such as Stage and Next Steps, and act “under the same permissions as the employee”.


**Control:** A suggestive mode where reps review, edit and approve updates, or an autonomous mode; testing and plan inspection in Agent Builder; Agentforce Observability; escalation to humans.


**Where it breaks:** Its strength is its boundary. Agents are deepest inside Salesforce, and data that lives outside it reaches them through Data 360 or MuleSoft. Pricing has several meters (Flex Credits, per-conversation, per-user add-ons), which makes a busy agent’s cost harder to predict.


**Pick it when:** Salesforce is your system of record and you want agents that write to it natively, under the same permissions and security as your reps.


## 5. HubSpot Breeze agents#


HubSpot sells Breeze agents as “always-on teammates”, managed from Agent Hub.


**How you build it:** Prebuilt agents (prospecting, customer and data) plus a custom agent builder, formerly Breeze Studio, where agents and workflows share one canvas. No coding required.


**What it reads and writes:** HubSpot CRM natively. The Prospecting Agent researches accounts, sources contacts through providers such as ZoomInfo and Apollo, enriches records and drafts emails. HubSpot’s pages do not say explicitly whether custom agents write to the CRM.


**Control:** Test before going live and choose which actions run without oversight. The Prospecting Agent can wait for review or send in an autonomous mode.


**Where it breaks:** Agents live inside HubSpot and are hosted only by HubSpot, so logic and data outside it are second-class. There is no code path to review or version an agent outside the product.


**Pick it when:** Your team runs on HubSpot and wants agents working on CRM data this week, with no integration project. Usage runs on HubSpot credits, and the Prospecting Agent is priced per lead.


## 6. Clay#


Clay’s agents are Claygent, for research inside tables, and Account Agents, which put “an expert AI agent on every account”.


**How you build it:** Describe the job in natural language; Claygent Builder generates the prompt and lets you test it across models, with saved test suites and every change versioned with rollback. Account Agents run a learn, decide, act loop with persistent memory, and became workflow steps in open beta in August 2026.


**What it reads and writes:** Account Agents read CRM, warehouse, call and email data, and write to the CRM or warehouse with human approval. General Claygents need CRM writes configured by hand.


**Control:** A full reasoning trace for each answer, test suites, versions and rollback.


**Where it breaks:** The agent’s home is still the table and the account record inside Clay. Versions govern each Clay artifact, not one source that versions the data model, the context, the agents and the activation together. Account Agents are in beta.


**Pick it when:** The agent’s job is research and enrichment across many accounts, and your team already works in Clay tables. Clay prices on actions and data credits with unlimited seats.


## 7. Lindy#


Lindy no longer sells an agent builder. It sells one “AI employee” you hire and teach.


**How you build it:** You do not, in the usual sense. Lindy knows 40+ jobs out of the box, learns new skills when you explain them in chat or show it a task once, and connects to hosted MCP servers. Its SDR role logs calls and deals in the CRM.


**What it reads and writes:** Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Attio and Close are among the 2,700+ apps it lists.


**Control:** “Anything with outside impact waits for your OK”, with configurable approvals; memory and apps are versioned; audit logs on Enterprise. Its pages describe no run tracing.


**Where it breaks:** One assistant shared by a team, not a system of agents you design. Its pages do not say how its CRM writes work action by action, which matters once it touches records other workflows depend on.


**Pick it when:** A non-technical rep wants to delegate work in Slack or chat today, with approval on anything that leaves the building. It costs a monthly fee per user plus credits.


## 8. Zapier#


Zapier’s agents now live as a single AI step inside the Zap editor, “AI by Zapier”.


**How you build it:** No code, helped by Copilot, with sales templates for meeting prep, qualification, and lead enrichment with outreach.


**What it reads and writes:** Whatever its 9,000+ app integrations reach. Its agents page names no CRM specifically.


**Control:** Require approval before a tool runs, read each run in Zap History with tools, inputs and outputs, and a per-run task cap that pauses for a human.


**Where it breaks:** A Zap sees the record that triggered it, one run at a time; the account behind it, its owner and its history are logic you build yourself. Pricing is in transition: the pricing page meters agent activities, while Zapier’s announcement moves agent cost to tasks.


**Pick it when:** Your team already runs on Zaps and wants an AI step in automations it has, with the broadest app catalog in this list.


## How to choose a platform for AI sales agents#


Start from the job, then check the four questions in order.


- **One rep, one task, this week:** Lindy, HubSpot Breeze or a Relevance AI template. Setup is minutes, and the cost of a wrong answer is one email a human reviews.
- **Agents inside your CRM:** Agentforce on Salesforce, Breeze on HubSpot. Native write-back and permissions beat any connector.
- **Research and enrichment at volume:** Clay, or Cargo when the results should feed scoring and routing that other systems share.
- **Self-hosted or fully custom:** n8n, if your team will own the data model.
- **Agents as part of the revenue engine:** Cargo, when agents should share one data model and one set of rules with your plays, be reviewed as code, and be traced run by run.


Then run the same test on any shortlist. Give the agent one real account and check four things: what it read, which tools it called, what it changed in your CRM, and whether you can see all three afterwards without asking the vendor. An agent you cannot read back is one you will end up supervising by hand.


Further reading on the same problem:[the agent-ready GTM platform](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/agent-ready-gtm-platform) ,[evaluating GTM agents before production](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/evaluate-go-to-market-agents-before-production) , and[AI agents for GTM](https://www.getcargo.ai/ai-agents-for-gtm) .


## Frequently asked questions#


An AI agent for sales is a model given a goal, tools and access to your data, which decides on its own which steps to take to reach the goal: for example researching an account, scoring it against your ICP, drafting a first email or updating the CRM. A workflow runs steps written in advance; an agent chooses them.


Yes. HubSpot Breeze, Relevance AI, Lindy and Zapier build agents without code, and Agentforce and Clay offer low-code builders. Code matters later, when several agents share data and rules and you want to review changes, version them and roll them back. Cargo and n8n support both paths.


Agentforce writes to Salesforce natively under the user’s permissions. n8n has native HubSpot and Salesforce nodes that create and update records. Cargo writes through maintained connectors with deduplication and protected fields. Clay Account Agents write with human approval. Check the vendor’s pages for the exact objects and actions before an agent touches records other workflows depend on.


A workflow executes the steps you defined after a trigger. An agent receives a goal and decides which tools to call and in what order. Most production sales systems use both: workflows for steps that must always happen the same way, agents for judgement such as research and qualification.


Give each agent one job (research, scoring, drafting), have them read the same account record and ICP definition, and keep a human approval on any step that changes the CRM or contacts a buyer. Relevance AI links agents on a visual canvas, n8n lets agents call sub-agents, Agentforce advertises multi-agent orchestration, and on Cargo agents run as steps in a play over one shared data model.


Run it on real accounts and check what it read, which tools it called, what it changed and whether you can see all three afterwards. Then test failure: a missing field, a duplicate record, an account owned by someone else. Look for approvals before actions, a run history, tests or evaluators, and a way to roll back a bad change.
